title.zh: 鑽探主權：跨國巨頭BP如何以化石資本資助印尼對西巴布亞的領土吞併
title.en: Drilling for Dominance: How Fossil Capital Subsidizes Indonesian Rule in West Papua

summary.zh:
【總結】本研究深入剖析了跨國能源巨頭英國石油公司（BP）與印尼國家機器在西巴布亞的政治經濟聯盟。BP旗下的「湯古液化天然氣項目」（Tangguh LNG）是印尼佔領的西巴布亞境內最大的資源開發項目。在過去十年間，印尼國內掀起強烈的「資源民族主義」浪潮，諸多外資主導的油氣礦產項目相繼遭到國有化，然而BP卻在2022年逆勢獲得長達20年的特許權延期至2043年。論文指出，這場持久跨國結盟並非偶然，而是因為化石資本不斷擴張的積累邏輯，與印尼身為後殖民定居殖民者對西巴布亞進行領土控制的野心形成了高度契合。這項開創性分析揭示了大型能源開發如何超越純粹的商業掠奪，成為主權國家深入邊疆、肢解原住民自決空間的制度性工具。

【研究問題】傳統政治經濟學與帝國主義批判多聚焦於西方列強在中東等地的資源掠奪，常將國家角色視為資本積累的外部保障者，且多數研究假設資源開採會必然引發中央集權式的財政抽乾。然而，學界鮮少探討「後殖民自決抗爭」（即新獨立國家轉過頭來殖民佔領其他邊陲領土，如印尼佔領西巴布亞）中，外國石油資本如何與佔領國的內部殖民戰略共謀。過去文獻常將西巴布亞的獨立運動簡化為受資源掠奪刺激的「邊緣反叛」，忽視了印尼國家如何主動利用油氣開發重構治理網絡。為何在印尼對外資充滿敵意並大力推行資源民族主義的背景下，BP能享有特權地位？國家領土控制與全球資本循環又是如何在具體制度中相互編織的？

【研究方法】作者結合批判地理學、馬克思主義政治經濟學與定居殖民主義理論，運用嚴謹的歷史檔案與財政數據進行實證分析。研究梳理了1960年代美印解密外交電報、美國國際開發署（USAID）檔案、BP歷年合約與人權監測報告，精準還原了自蘇卡諾、蘇哈托時期以來油氣合約與西巴布亞主權歸屬相互交易的歷史脈絡。方法上的核心創新在於，作者將2001年印尼民主轉型期同步頒布的兩部關鍵法律——規範外資准入的第22號《石油與天然氣法》以及旨在安撫分離勢力的第21號《特別自治法》（OTSUS）——置於同一分析框架下，追蹤「產量分成合約」（PSC）機制如何與地方財政轉移支付結合，並利用印尼中央統計局（BPS）的行政區劃演變數據，實證檢驗油氣收益如何轉化為國家的實體統治架構。

【結果】研究揭示了令人震驚的共謀細節：在湯古項目開發之初，丹那美拉村（Tanah Merah）的原住民土地權（hak ulayat）被強行剝奪，當地氏族僅獲象徵性的51,990美元補償（僅佔初始資本支出的0.005%），後續抗議更遭到BP出資雇傭的印尼軍警強力鎮壓。與傳統「中央吸乾地方」的資源掠奪模式相反，《特別自治法》出台後，印尼將高達70%的國家油氣收益返還給西巴布亞地方政府（以項目所在地的賓圖尼灣縣為例，2019年非稅資源分成達9938億印尼盾，約6330萬美元，佔其平衡基金絕大部分）。然而，巨額收益未有一分一毫直達原住民，而是被用於推動「行政區劃分裂」（pemekaran）：西巴布亞的省份從1至2個拆分為6個，鄉鎮級行政區自2004年的252個暴增至2025年的799個，基層村落擴張至7548個。這些由BP天然氣收入資助的官僚機構，不僅養活了龐大的公務員群體並引發外島移民浪潮，更在客觀上將印尼的軍事監控與行政觸角深深嵌入原住民土地，完美達成了「不戰而屈人之兵」的殖民壓制。
summary.en:
**Summary:** Naish Gawen provides a compelling critique of the long-standing alliance between multinational energy giant British Petroleum (BP) and the Indonesian state in West Papua. Focusing on the Tangguh Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) project—the largest resource extraction enterprise in the Indonesian-occupied region—the article demonstrates how the economic logic of global capital accumulation operates in lockstep with the state's settler-colonial logic of territorial consolidation. At a time when Indonesia has aggressively pursued resource nationalism by expropriating and taking over foreign-run concessions across the archipelago, BP achieved a rare and historic 20-year production contract extension through 2043. Gawen reveals that Tangguh LNG has not simply served as an offshore enclave for corporate extraction; its revenue architecture has been deliberately repurposed by Jakarta to finance the proliferation of sub-national administrative units, functionally cementing state control over indigenous lands and dampening the Papuan struggle for self-determination.

**Problem:** Conventional scholarship on the geopolitics of fossil fuels largely focuses on Western imperialism in the Middle East or analyzes resource governance through the narrow prism of the "resource curse," where conflict is viewed merely as a reactionary grievance against environmental and distributive injustice. Moreover, theoretical debates in Marxist political economy (such as Ellen Meiksins Wood versus David Harvey) have frequently disputed whether state-territorial imperatives necessarily coincide with the expansion of capitalist accumulation. In the context of post-colonial self-determination struggles—where formerly colonized states replicate colonial occupations over peripheral populations—the precise mechanics connecting foreign resource extraction to state territorialization remain critically undertheorized. The study asks: How has a foreign petroleum conglomerate maintained privileged institutional standing inside a fiercely nationalist regime, and through what concrete fiscal and spatial channels do oil and gas flows facilitate modern territorial conquest?

**Approach:** Gawen employs a qualitative and descriptive quantitative methodology rooted in critical political geography and historical political economy. The research triangulates declassified US State Department cables from the 1960s, Indonesian legislative acts, budgetary records from the central government and local regencies, corporate social responsibility reports, independent human rights audits, and demographic data from the Indonesian Central Bureau of Statistics (BPS). Conceptually, Gawen innovates by juxtaposing two defining reform packages passed concurrently in 2001 during Indonesia's *Reformasi* era: Law No. 22 on Oil and Gas (which deregulated the sector following IMF mandates) and Law No. 21 on Special Autonomy for Papua (OTSUS). By dissecting the Production Sharing Contract (PSC) terms and fiscal equalization frameworks, the author traces the precise pathway through which offshore gas extraction subsidizes the administrative fracturing and territorial policing of indigenous territory.

**Results:** The findings document the foundational violence and institutional engineering underpinning Tangguh LNG. During the initial onshore acquisition, indigenous Papuan clans in Tanah Merah village had their customary land tenure (*hak ulayat*) permanently extinguished in exchange for a paltry collective sum of $51,990—constituting a negligible 0.005% of initial capital expenditure—while community blockades were suppressed by state security forces directly subsidized by BP. Crucially, confounding traditional assumptions that resource peripheries are merely starved of capital by the core, Indonesia's Special Autonomy framework redirected 70% of state oil and gas revenues directly back to sub-national governments in West Papua (in Teluk Bintuni regency, non-tax natural resource revenues accounted for 993.8 billion IDR or roughly $63.3 million in 2019). However, zero percent flows directly to customary landowners. Instead, this influx financed an explosive administrative fragmentation (*pemekaran*): between 2004 and 2025, West Papuan districts expanded from 252 to 799, and recognized villages climbed from 3,782 to 7,548 across six newly partitioned provinces. This proliferation of bureaucracy and civil service salaries catalyzed demographic displacement via transmigrant settlement, demonstrating that fossil capital serves as the vital financial engine consolidating Indonesia's settler-colonial occupation.

keyArticle.title: Capital accumulation and territorial control in West Papua's offshore gas industry
